name: Heroin (diamorphine)
summary: Heroin is barely a drug in its own right. Its half-life is two to six minutes, because it is not meant to last — the two acetyl groups exist only to get morphine across the blood-brain barrier, which it does roughly a hundred times faster than morphine manages alone. Once inside, it is stripped back to morphine. Heroin is a delivery mechanism for a drug that was already available.
mechanism: Deacetylated to 6-monoacetylmorphine within minutes, then to morphine, both mu-opioid agonists. The fat-solubility added by the acetyl groups is the whole invention: the same receptor, the same final molecule, reached in seconds instead of half an hour. The rush is a kinetic phenomenon, not a pharmacological one.
model_note: Heroin itself is too short-lived to plot usefully, so this curve tracks morphine-equivalent concentration — what the receptors are actually seeing after the cascade. The onset reflects heroin's speed across the barrier; the decay reflects morphine's clearance.

iv.note: Reaches the brain in 15-30 seconds. The entire dose arrives at once, which is both the appeal and the reason this route carries the highest overdose risk — there is no opportunity to notice it is too much.

smoked.note: Vaporised and inhaled. Nearly as fast as injection but with a lower peak and significant losses, which makes the margin for error wider.

insufflated.note: Slower, lower peak, less abrupt onset.

oral.note: Heavy first-pass metabolism converts it straight to morphine before it reaches the circulation, so taken orally heroin is simply a weak, slow dose of morphine with none of the characteristic onset.

pathways.name: 6-MAM
pathways.note: The intermediate, and the only metabolite unique to heroin — it is what distinguishes heroin use from morphine use in toxicology. Half-life around 6-25 minutes.

pathways.name: Morphine
pathways.note: The species that does nearly all the work. Everything after the first few minutes is a morphine curve.

pathways.name: Morphine-3-glucuronide
pathways.note: Inactive at the opioid receptor but neuroexcitatory; implicated in the agitation and myoclonus seen at high doses.

pathways.name: Morphine-6-glucuronide
pathways.note: More potent than morphine and cleared by the kidneys. In renal impairment it accumulates over days, which is a classic cause of delayed, unexplained opioid overdose.

effect_levels.label: 50 µg/L — marked sedation and respiratory slowing
100 µg/L — range reported in fatal cases in non-tolerant users

risk: Tolerance falls far faster than it builds. After a break of even one to two weeks — detox, prison, hospital, illness — a previously ordinary dose can be fatal. This is the single most common fatal pattern in opioid use, and the curve here does not change while the person's tolerance does.
Street supply is not standardised. The same measured amount can vary several-fold in purity between batches, and fentanyl contamination makes the real dose unknowable from appearance.

Combined with any other depressant — alcohol, benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids — respiratory depression is more than additive. The large majority of opioid deaths involve a second depressant. See interactions.
Naloxone reverses it, but its half-life is shorter than the opioid's: someone revived can slip back into overdose as the naloxone wears off, especially with long-acting opioids.
Using alone is what turns an overdose into a death. An overdose is survivable if someone is there.
